title: More Than One Choice

content.title: What Happens When the `if` Is False?
content.summary: `else` runs when the `if` condition is false — it's the fallback path.
content.body: In the last lesson, when the player typed something that didn't match, the program just went silent. That works sometimes — but usually you want to say something either way. That's what `else` is for. `else` runs when the `if` condition is false.

content.title: `if` / `else`: Two Paths
content.summary: `if` handles the "yes" path; `else` handles everything else.
content.note: Now the program always has something to say. One path for `"yes"`, one path for everything else. The player never gets silence.

content.title: `else` Has No Condition
content.summary: `else` doesn't check anything — it just runs when nothing above matched.
content.body: Notice that `else` doesn't have a condition after it — just a colon. It's the "catch-all" — it runs whenever the `if` was false. You can only have one `else` per `if`, and it always goes at the end.

content.title: Story Branches
content.summary: `if`/`else` is the engine behind choose-your-own-adventure stories.
content.body: Every choose-your-own-adventure story is secretly just a bunch of `if`/`else` statements! One choice sends you down one path, the other choice sends you down another.
content.note:
You're writing a game engine now. 🎮

Not into dragons? `if`/`else` works for any choice — `pizza or sushi`, `forest or city`, `morning or night`. The story can be anything.

editorPrompt: Write an `if`/`else` so the program always has something to say.
progressiveHints:
# Hint: else goes after the if block, no condition needed
# if answer == "something":
#     print("matched!")
# else:
#     print("didn't match")
challenge: 🚀 Dive Deeper: Write a two-path mini adventure. Ask the player to choose between two options (a forest or a castle, a spaceship or a submarine — your choice!). Write a different story outcome for each path with at least 2 `print()` lines each.
